blocks.text: A test rig blends a load-cell signal and a position-sensor signal into one weighted measurement, filters out motor noise above a kilohertz, and rejects the 50 Hz hum that the long sensor cable picks up. Three small op-amp circuits, each built from a handful of resistors and one capacitor, do all of it before the signal reaches the ADC.

blocks.markdown: The ideal op-amp rules (no input current; $v_+=v_-$ under negative feedback) analyse every circuit here. The circuits are all variations on the inverting and non-inverting amplifiers of the previous unit, with extra inputs or a capacitor in the feedback path.

blocks.title: Summing (inverting) amplifier
blocks.text: Several sources $v_1,v_2,\dots$ connect through resistors $R_1,R_2,\dots$ to the inverting node; the feedback resistor $R_f$ connects output to that node and the $(+)$ input is grounded. Each input sees its own gain $-R_f/R_k$ and the contributions add.

blocks.caption: Summing amplifier: because the inverting node is a virtual ground, each input current v_k/R_k adds in R_f independently

blocks.title: Summing two sensor signals
blocks.prompt: Combine sensor 1 with weight 2 and sensor 2 with weight 0.5 (output inverted), using $R_f=100$ k$\Omega$. Choose $R_1$, $R_2$ and find the output for $v_1=0.30$ V and $v_2=1.20$ V.
blocks.answer: R_1 = 50 kohm, R_2 = 200 kohm; v_o = -1.20 V. Each sensor contributes -0.60 V.

blocks.markdown: **Active low-pass filter.** Place a capacitor $C$ in parallel with the feedback resistor $R_f$ of an inverting amplifier. At low frequency the capacitor is an open circuit and the gain is $-R_f/R_{in}$. As frequency rises, $C$ offers a lower impedance $1/(j\omega C)$ in parallel with $R_f$, so the gain falls. The **cut-off frequency** $f_c$ is where the gain magnitude has fallen to $1/\sqrt2$ (-3 dB) of its low-frequency value, and the filter has a single pole: the gain falls by about 20 dB per decade above $f_c$.

blocks.caption: First-order active low-pass filter, inverting configuration

blocks.title: Cut-off frequency
blocks.prompt: An inverting low-pass stage has $R_{in}=5.0$ k$\Omega$, $R_f=15$ k$\Omega$ and $C=10$ nF across $R_f$. Find the DC gain, $f_c$ and the gain magnitude at $f_c$.

steps.text: Cut-off frequency from the feedback network.
At $f_c$ the gain magnitude is down by $\sqrt2$.

blocks.answer: DC gain -3.0, f_c = 1.06 kHz, and |G| = 2.12 at f_c. Note that f_c depends on R_f and C but not on R_in.

blocks.markdown: **Difference amplifier.** A signal sensor often has two output wires, and noise (mains hum, ground shifts) appears equally on both. The wanted signal is their **difference** $v_d=v_2-v_1$; the unwanted noise is the **common-mode** voltage $v_{cm}=(v_1+v_2)/2$. A difference amplifier uses $R_1$ from $v_1$ to the inverting input, $R_2$ in feedback, $R_3$ from $v_2$ to the non-inverting input and $R_4$ from that input to ground. If $R_2/R_1=R_4/R_3$, the output is $v_o=(R_2/R_1)(v_2-v_1)$: the common-mode term cancels exactly.

blocks.caption: Difference amplifier with matched resistor ratios

items: Every input of a summing amplifier is isolated by the virtual ground; inputs do not interact.
The filter's $f_c$ is set by $R_f C$, and its pass-band gain by $R_f/R_{in}$; they can be set independently.
Resistor mismatch of 1 % in a difference amplifier can leave a common-mode gain of order 1 % of the signal gain.
The common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) is the ratio of differential gain to common-mode gain; higher is better.

blocks.title: Matched resistors give common-mode rejection
blocks.text: A difference amplifier rejects common-mode noise only if $R_2/R_1=R_4/R_3$ closely. Use 0.1 % resistors or an integrated instrumentation amplifier for demanding sensors.

points: Active low-pass: $f_c=1/(2\pi R_fC)$, pass-band gain $-R_f/R_{in}$, gain $1/\sqrt2$ of that at $f_c$.
Difference amplifier: $v_o=(R_2/R_1)(v_2-v_1)$ and common-mode voltage cancels when the ratios match.

questions.stem: A summing amplifier has $R_1=R_2=R_f=10$ k$\Omega$. The inputs are 1.0 V and 2.0 V. What is the output?

distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this averages the inputs, which a summer does not do.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this ignores the 1.0 V input.

questions.explanation: With all resistors equal each input has gain $-1$ and the outputs add: $v_o=-(1.0+2.0)=-3.0$ V.

questions.stem: An inverting low-pass filter has $R_f=1.6$ k$\Omega$ in parallel with $C=100$ nF. What is its cut-off frequency?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: 1/(RC) = 6250 rad/s, not hertz, leaving out 2 pi.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this uses 10 k instead of 1.6 k.

questions.explanation: $f_c=1/(2\pi R_fC)=1/(2\pi\times1600\times10^{-7})=995$ Hz. The input resistor does not enter the cut-off frequency.

options.text: A voltage that appears equally on both inputs of a differential amplifier
The voltage difference between the two inputs

questions.correctOptionText: A voltage that appears equally on both inputs of a differential amplifier

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it is the same on both inputs, e.g. mains hum on both wires.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is the differential (wanted) signal.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the supply is not an input signal.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: offset is an output error, not an input signal type.

questions.explanation: A common-mode voltage is the part shared by both inputs, such as noise picked up equally by a twin-wire cable. An ideal difference amplifier responds only to the difference.

questions.stem: Using $R_f=30$ k$\Omega$, which input resistors give $v_o=-(3v_1+2v_2)$ in a summing amplifier?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this multiplies R_f by the weights.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this uses the weights as kilohm values.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this swaps the two resistors, giving weights 2 and 3.

questions.explanation: The gain for each input is $R_f/R_k$, so $R_k=R_f/\text{weight}$: $30/3=10$ k$\Omega$ for input 1 and $30/2=15$ k$\Omega$ for input 2.

questions.stem: In a difference amplifier, why must $R_2/R_1=R_4/R_3$ be maintained closely?

options.text: Otherwise a part of the common-mode input appears at the output
Otherwise the op-amp would saturate for all inputs
Otherwise the input current becomes infinite
Otherwise the differential gain becomes zero

questions.correctOptionText: Otherwise a part of the common-mode input appears at the output

distractorRationale.a: Correct: mismatch makes the two input paths gain differently, so common-mode voltage leaks through.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: saturation depends on signal levels and gain, not ratio matching.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the ideal op-amp input current is zero regardless.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: differential gain is not zero for a mismatch; rejection is the problem.

questions.explanation: Cancellation depends on both inputs experiencing equal gain to the common-mode voltage. Mismatched ratios give unequal gains, leaving a residual common-mode term at the output.

questions.stem: A summing amplifier has $R_f=47$ k$\Omega$, $R_1=22$ k$\Omega$ and $R_2=10$ k$\Omega$. The inputs are $v_1=0.50$ V and $v_2=0.20$ V. What is the output voltage in volts?
questions.explanation: $v_o=-47(0.50/22+0.20/10)=-47(0.02273+0.02000)=-2.008$ V. Each term is an input current in mA that flows through $R_f$.

An inverting low-pass stage has $R_{in}=10$ k$\Omega$, $R_f=100$ k$\Omega$ and $C=1.0$ nF across $R_f$. What is the magnitude of its gain at 8.0 kHz?
A strain-gauge bridge is connected to an amplifier by a 10 m twin cable running beside a motor. Explain how a difference amplifier removes the mains pick-up and what limits how well it does so.
markingGuide: Pick-up appears equally on both wires: a common-mode signal
The bridge signal appears as a difference between the wires
Difference amplifier output depends on v2 - v1 so the common-mode part cancels
Cancellation requires matched resistor ratios R2/R1 = R4/R3
Mismatch or finite CMRR leaves a residual common-mode error; use precise resistors or an instrumentation amplifier
questions.explanation: Noise from the motor and mains couples equally into both cable wires, so it is a common-mode voltage, while the bridge signal appears as the difference between them. A difference amplifier outputs $(R_2/R_1)(v_2-v_1)$, so the common-mode part cancels provided $R_2/R_1=R_4/R_3$. Resistor mismatch and finite CMRR leave a small residual error.

questions.stem: Design a summing amplifier (using $R_f=100$ k$\Omega$) with $v_o=-(0.5v_1+2v_2)$. Give $R_1$ and $R_2$, find the output for $v_1=4.0$ V and $v_2=0.50$ V, and explain why the two inputs do not interfere with each other.
markingGuide: The inverting node is a virtual ground, so each input current is v_k/R_k independent of the other source
The input currents add at the node and flow through R_f
questions.explanation: Each weight is $R_f/R_k$, so $R_1=100/0.5=200$ k$\Omega$ and $R_2=100/2=50$ k$\Omega$. The output is $-(0.5\times4.0+2\times0.5)=-3.0$ V. The inverting node is held at virtual ground by feedback, so each source drives only its own resistor with current $v_k/R_k$, and these currents simply add in $R_f$.
